items.title: A test file for the pricer library
items.prose: The desk's pricer library is hidden: `bs_call`, `bs_put`, `bs_delta_call` and `tree_call`. Write its test file with the test kit from l12: at least six tests covering a limit, put-call parity, a known value, the tree's convergence and delta by bumping. Check runs your file against the correct library and against six versions with one bug each, including a call that returns 0 when $\sigma < 0.001$.
items.question: Write the test file.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Test 1 needs at least six tests, all passing on the correct library. Tests 2 to 7 each swap in one bug (put with $N(d_2)$, put or call without the discount, a call that is 0 below $\sigma = 0.001$, a tree stuck at 64 steps, a discounted delta) and need at least one of your tests to fail. The example expects exactly six tests.

feedback.correct: Six independent checks; every planted bug trips at least one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the PASS and FAIL lines under the first failing row.

byKey.test-1: On the correct library you need at least six tests and no failures. Check each tolerance against the error the quantity really has.
byKey.test-5: The call that returns 0 at tiny volatility got through. You need a $\sigma \to 0$ limit test.
byKey.test-6: The tree stuck at 64 steps (0.031 off) got through. Test the tree at $n = 512$ within 0.01.
byKey.test-7: The discounted delta (0.6058) got through. Compare `bs_delta_call` with a central difference within 1e-5.

explain.text: Each family catches different bugs: parity and known values catch formula slips, the limit catches special-case code, convergence catches the tree, the bump catches a Greek. A suite earns trust when every plausible bug fails at least one test.

items.title: A packed lattice for an American put
items.prose: A square $(n + 1)^2$ lattice wastes almost half its places. Pack the triangle instead: node $(i, j)$ at $i(i + 1)/2 + j$, $(n + 1)(n + 2)/2$ nodes in all. Store every share price in one vector filled with `push_back` after a single `reserve`, with no `pow` per node, then price the American put on it.
items.question: Write `flat_american_put`. At $S = K = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$, $T = 1$ and $n = 512$ it is £6.0889.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and its first compile takes 10 to 15 s; later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Eight hidden tests: prices for $n$ from 1 to 1,000 and strikes £90 to £150 within a relative 1e-9, and the packed index of node (3, 2).

feedback.correct: One reserved block of share prices, half the memory of the square lattice, and the same American price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: At $n = 4$ the put is 5.8828. Check row $i$ starts at $S d^i$ and climbs by $u^2$, and that `v` reads row `i + 1`.
byKey.test-6: Deep in the money the put is worth exercising at once: £50. The early-exercise value is `k - price[tri(i, j)]`.

explain.text: `reserve` makes one allocation of the exact size, so the `push_back` loop never copies. Row $i$ starts at index $i(i + 1)/2$ because rows $0$ to $i - 1$ hold $1 + 2 + \dots + i$ nodes. At $n = 1{,}000$ that is 501,501 doubles per vector, against 1,002,001 for the square.

items.title: Hunting a regression
items.prose: Last night the regression test `cpp_matches_python` started failing. It passed on the release tagged three weeks ago, and 64 commits have landed since. You will find the commit that broke it by halving the range.
items.question: Put the steps in order.

lines.text: Confirm the test fails on today's commit: mark it bad
Confirm it passes on the tagged release: mark it good
Check out the commit halfway between good and bad
Build it and run only the failing test
Mark that commit good or bad, halving the range; repeat from the halfway step
When one commit is left, read its diff and write a test that pins the bug

feedback.correct: Six halvings find one commit among 64.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need a good and a bad end before you can halve.

explain.text: `git bisect` automates exactly this: `git bisect bad`, `git bisect good v1.4`, then a build and test at each step. 64 commits take $\log_2 64 = 6$ builds. The final test pins the bug so it cannot return unnoticed.

items.title: The timing write-up for the desk
items.prompt:
This is the exit deliverable of the C++ topic. Write a one-page note to the desk head comparing the Python tree pricer (trees course) with your C++ version. Use these medians for one 1,000-step European call on a Linux server (Intel Xeon, 2.1 GHz, Python 3.13, g++ 13.3): Python loop 40 ms; NumPy 4.2 ms; C++ `-O0` 4.5 ms; C++ `-O2` 0.45 ms. The American put took 15.5 ms with `pow` at every node and 1.6 ms with one `pow` per step, both at `-O2`. The desk prices 100,000 options a night.

Cover: your method, the numbers, the flags and machine, how you know the two pricers agree, the caveats, and what you recommend.
items.model:
**Method.** I timed the European call at $S = K = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$, $T = 1$ on a 1,000-step CRR tree. Both versions run the same algorithm: one row of $n + 1$ values, reused at each step. Each run starts with one warm-up call. I then timed five batches (C++: batches long enough to span many clock ticks) and report the median per tree. Every timed price went into a sum that is printed, so nothing was optimised away. Before timing, the C++ and Python prices were checked to agree to a relative $10^{-9}$ on 100 seeded random inputs.

**Machine and builds.** One Linux server, Intel Xeon at 2.1 GHz, idle apart from the benchmark. Python 3.13, pure Python lists. NumPy version vectorising each step. C++ built with g++ 13.3, `-std=c++17`, at `-O0` and at `-O2` (the desk's release flags).

**Numbers (median per tree, $n = 1{,}000$).**

| Version | ms per tree | vs Python |
|---|---|---|
| Python loop | 40 | 1× |
| NumPy | 4.2 | 10× |
| C++ `-O0` | 4.5 | 9× |
| C++ `-O2` | 0.45 | about 90× |

Time grows about 4 times per doubling of $n$ in both languages, as $n^2/2$ node updates predict, so the ratio holds across $n$.

**What it means for the batch.** 100,000 options a night take $100{,}000 \times 0.040 = 4{,}000$ s, about 67 minutes, in Python, and 45 s in the C++ release build. The American put shows a second lesson: with `pow` at every node it took 15.5 ms at `-O2`; with one `pow` per step 1.6 ms. The algorithm change was worth as much as the language change.

**Caveats.** One machine; another processor or compiler will change the numbers, though not the order of magnitude. The machine was shared, so single runs scattered by up to 50%; the median of five absorbs most of it. The browser runs of the course were slower again (WebAssembly, a 100 µs clock). I did not test `-O3` or `-march=native` in production; `-O3` was faster here, but it is not what we ship. No `-ffast-math`: it changes prices in the last digits and can delete NaN checks.

**Recommendation.** Move the nightly tree pricing to the C++ library built `RelWithDebInfo` (`-O2 -g -DNDEBUG`), keeping the Python pricer as the reference in a regression test (100 seeded inputs, relative $10^{-9}$). Run the test suite on Debug and Release in CI. Re-run this benchmark on the production machine before sizing the batch window, and publish it with the machine, compiler and flags.

rubric.text: Method: same algorithm and inputs, warm-up, repeated batches, median, results kept alive (a printed sink)
States the machine, compiler and flags for every number
Numbers right: about 90 times faster at `-O2`; Python batch about 67 minutes against 45 s
Notes that `-O0` and NumPy are about ten times slower than `-O2`, so a debug build must not be quoted
Shows the two pricers agree, with a tolerance (relative 1e-9) and not `==`
Mentions the algorithm change (one `pow` per step) as a gain no flag gives
Caveats: one machine, noise, illustrative numbers; no `-ffast-math`
A concrete recommendation: the build type to ship, the regression test to keep, and a re-run on the production machine

items.title: How fine a tree fits the window
items.prose: The C++ release build prices one 1,000-step tree in 0.45 ms. The 100,000-option batch must finish in 30 minutes on one core. Time per tree grows as $n^2$.
items.question: What is the largest number of steps $n$ the batch can afford?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the time allowed per option, then use $T \propto n^2$.

byKey.lin: You scaled $n$ by 40, as if time grew in proportion to $n$. It grows as $n^2$, so $n$ grows by $\sqrt{40}$.
byKey.sec: Check the units: 30 minutes is 1,800 s, so each option may take 18 ms.

explain.text: Per option: $1{,}800\ \text{s} / 100{,}000 = 18$ ms, which is $18 / 0.45 = 40$ times the 1,000-step time. Since $T \propto n^2$, $n = 1{,}000\sqrt{40} \approx 6{,}325$.

items.title: A lattice read the wrong way
items.prose:
A colleague's flat lattice stores node $(i, j)$ at `v[i * (n + 1) + j]`, but their backward step reads

```cpp
for (int j = 0; j <= i; ++j)
    v[j * (n + 1) + i] = disc * (q * v[(j + 1) * (n + 1) + i + 1]
                             + (1 - q) * v[j * (n + 1) + i + 1]);
```

The leaves were written with the first index.
items.question: What goes wrong?

options.text: It reads nodes the leaves never filled, so the price is wrong, and each step jumps a whole row in memory
Only speed: the price is right, but the inner loop has a stride of $n + 1$
options.why: Swapping $i$ and $j$ in the index reads different nodes, not the same nodes in a different order. The leaves sit in row $n$, which this code never reads.

options.text: Nothing: $i$ and $j$ play the same part in a square lattice
options.why: Row $i$ is a step of the tree; column $j$ counts ups. They are not interchangeable.

options.text: It always crashes with an index out of range
options.why: Every index stays below $(n + 1)^2$, so no check fires: the code quietly prices from empty nodes.

feedback.correct: Wrong price and a strided walk: the swapped index costs both.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where did the leaves go, and where does this code read?

explain.text: The leaves are at `n * (n + 1) + j`, but this loop reads places such as `j * (n + 1) + n` and writes column `i`. The result is a wrong price, and the inner loop jumps $n + 1$ doubles per step. An `index(i, j, cols)` helper used everywhere prevents both.

items.title: A benchmark to fix
items.question: Which problems does this benchmark have? Select all that apply.

options.text: It times a single, cold run with no warm-up or repeats
It uses `system_clock`, which can jump, instead of `steady_clock`
The price is never used, so an optimised build may delete the call
Printing with `std::cout` after the second reading slows the timed call
options.why: The print happens after `b` is read, outside the timed interval. Printing inside the interval would be a problem.

feedback.correct: Four problems; the print is outside the interval.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the build, the clock, the repetition and what happens to the result.

explain.text: Fix: build with `-O2`, use `steady_clock` and `duration_cast<microseconds>`, warm up, time five batches of many trees, add every price to a printed sink, and report the median per tree. Printing after the second reading is fine; flushing output inside the interval would not be.

items.title: Scanning an order book
items.prose: An order book keeps 10,000 price levels as `std::vector<Level>`, where `struct Level { double price; double qty; int orders; int flags; };` is 24 bytes. A risk check scans only the `qty` of every level.
items.question: How many 64-byte cache lines does the scan read?

feedback.correct: 3,750 lines; a separate `qty` vector would need 1,250.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The distance from one `qty` to the next is a whole `Level`.

byKey.soa: 1,250 is the count for a separate `qty` vector. Here each quantity drags its price, order count and flags along.
byKey.each: Two or three levels share each line, so it is fewer than one line per level.

explain.text: $10{,}000 \times 24 / 64 = 3{,}750$ lines. Stored as a struct of arrays, the `qty` column alone is $10{,}000 \times 8 / 64 = 1{,}250$ lines, three times fewer.
